title: 04 Linear Regression: Flexibility
text:
3. Overfitting: Can We Do Better?
Adding \(x^2\) seemed to help, can we do even better by adding \(x^3, x^4, \dots\) ?
Higher polynomial powers add more basis vectors to \(\mathbf{X}\),


Flexible Models
x_min, x_max = x_data.min(), x_data.max()
x_norm = (x_data - x_min) / (x_max - x_min)
x_grid_500 = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 500)
u_grid = (x_grid_500 - x_min) / (x_max - x_min)

degrees = [2, 15]
colors = ['#2ca02c', '#8c564b']
ss_tot = np.sum((y_data - np.mean(y_data))**2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.scatter(x_data, y_data, color='#1f77b4', s=50, edgecolors='k', zorder=5)

for deg, col in zip(degrees, colors):
    X_d = np.column_stack([x_norm**k for k in range(deg + 1)])
    theta_d, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_d, y_data, rcond=None)
    y_pred_train = X_d @ theta_d
    ss_res = np.sum((y_data - y_pred_train)**2)
    r2 = 1.0 - (ss_res / ss_tot)
    X_grid = np.column_stack([u_grid**k for k in range(deg + 1)])
    y_pred_grid = X_grid @ theta_d
    ax.plot(x_grid_500, y_pred_grid, color=col, lw=2.2, label=f'Degree {deg} ($R^2 = {r2:.4f}$)')

ax.axhline(0, color='gray', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_ylim(-12, 30)
ax.set_title('Too Much Flexibility?', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
ax.legend(fontsize=10, loc='upper left')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 4: Comparing Model Complexity: As the number of parameters increases, the model can fit sample-specific noise (overfitting).






3.1 Signatures of Overfitting
To force a high-degree polynomial through noisy data points, adjacent terms must oscillate with large opposing magnitudes. Below we compare the fitted weights for Degree 2 versus Degree 15:


Inspect Parameter Weights for Degree 2 vs. Degree 15
X_2 = np.column_stack([x_norm**k for k in range(3)])
th_2, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_2, y_data, rcond=None)
norm_2 = np.linalg.norm(th_2)

X_15 = np.column_stack([x_norm**k for k in range(16)])
th_15, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_15, y_data, rcond=None)
norm_15 = np.linalg.norm(th_15)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.0))

# Panel 1: Degree 2
axes[0].bar(range(len(th_2)), th_2, color='#2ca02c', alpha=0.85, edgecolor='k', width=0.5)
axes[0].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.8, linestyle='--')
axes[0].set_xticks(range(len(th_2)))
axes[0].set_xticklabels([f"$\\theta_{{{k}}}$" for k in range(len(th_2))])

axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Panel 2: Degree 15

            alpha=0.85, edgecolor='k', width=0.6)

Figure 5: Parameter Weight Explosion: In Degree 2 (left), weights are modest and relatively stable. In Degree 15 (right), adjacent weights explode to billions, alternating in sign to fit noise fluctuations.





As the polynomial degree \(d\) increases, three coupled mathematical phenomena emerge simultaneously:

Training Error (\(\text{RSS} \to 0\)): Residual Sum of Squares plunges as the model interpolates noise.
Gram Matrix Invertibility (\(\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) \to 0\)): Columns become nearly collinear, flattening the spanned parallelotope.
Parameter Explosion (\(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\| \to \infty\)): The Euclidean norm shoots up exponentially.



Generate Overfitting Diagnostic Dashboard
degs = list(range(2, 16))

det_vals = []

title: 04 Linear Regression: Flexibility
text:
4. Summary

Feature Engineering Unlocks Flexibility: One-hot dummy coding and polynomial basis expansions allow linear regression models to fit qualitative groups and non-linear curves while remaining strictly linear in the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\).
OLS Orthogonality vs. Underfitting: The normal equations guarantee \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}\), but systematic trends in the residual patterns may signal underfitting.
Signatures of Overfitting: Adding unchecked polynomial degrees drives training RSS towards zero, but collapses \(\det(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) \to 0\) and causes parameter weights to explode into destructive alternating competition (\(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\| \to \infty\)).
Controlling Flexibility: The explosive growth of \(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\|\) motivates regularization strategies and adjustments to the loss function.

title: 06 Logistic Regression: Classification
text:
2. Modeling Expectations and Probabilities
When the target is a boolean label \(y \in \{0, 1\}\), each observation conditioned on \(x\) follows a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y & \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
P(Y=y|p) & = \begin{cases}
              p   & y = 1 (\mathtt{TRUE}) \\
              1-p & y = 0 (\mathtt{FALSE})
          \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
We assume that success probability \(p\) is a function of observable features, i.e. \(p = p(x)\).
For a given value of \(x\), the conditional expectation is precisely the probability of the positive class:
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=x] &= \sum_{y} y \cdot P(Y = y \mid X=x) \\
&= 1 \cdot P(Y = 1 \mid X=x) + 0 \cdot P(Y = 0 \mid X=x) \\
&= P(Y = 1 \mid X=x) \\
&= p(x) = ?
\end{aligned}\]
c.f. linear regression: \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=x] = x^T \theta\)
Similarly, the conditional variance is:
\[\text{Var}[Y \mid X=x] = p(x)(1 - p(x))\]


Bernoulli Variance Curve
p_vals = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
var_vals = p_vals * (1 - p_vals)

Mapping Probabilities to an Unbounded Scale
Which functions should we allow for \(p(x) \in (0,1)\)?
To connect an unbounded linear combination \(z = x^T \theta \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) to a valid probability \(p \in (0, 1)\), we transition across three distinct scales:









Scale
Definition
Domain / Range





Probability
\(p(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid x)\)
\([0, 1]\)



Odds
\(\text{odds}(x) = \frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)}\)
\([0, \infty)\)



Log-Odds (Logit)
\(\text{logit}(p) = \ln\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\)
\((-\infty, +\infty)\)






The Sigmoid Link Function
Now the log-odds can be modeled as a linear regression of the features:
\[\ln\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = z = x^T \theta\]
Then \(p(x)\) can be written as the logistic (sigmoid) function:
\[p(x) = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]


Plot Logistic Sigmoid Function

NoteEssential Properties of the Sigmoid Function




Symmetry: \(\sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z)\)
Boundary Limits: \(\lim_{z \to +\infty} \sigma(z) = 1\) and \(\lim_{z \to -\infty} \sigma(z) = 0\)
Center Point: \(\sigma(0) = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = 0.5\)
Derivative:
\[\frac{d\sigma}{dz} = \sigma(z)\left(1 - \sigma(z)\right)\]

text:
4. Interpreting Parameters and Odds Ratios
In linear regression; coefficient \(\theta_j\) represents the additive change in \(y\) when predictor \(x_j\) changes by one unit, holding all other predictors constant.
In logistic regression, \(\theta_j\) represents the change in the odds ratio when predictor \(x_j\) changes by one unit, holding all other predictors constant (\(z_2 = z_1 + \theta_j \Delta x_j = z_1 + \theta_j\)):
\[\text{Odds Ratio} = \frac{\text{Odds}(x_j + 1)}{\text{Odds}(x_j)} = e^{z_2} / e^{z_1} = e^{z_2 - z_1} = e^{\theta_j}\]

\(\theta_j = 0 \implies \text{Odds Ratio} = 1\): Feature \(x_j\) has no association with the odds of disease.
\(\theta_j > 0 \implies \text{Odds Ratio} > 1\): Feature \(x_j\) increases the odds.
\(\theta_j < 0 \implies \text{Odds Ratio} < 1\): Feature \(x_j\) decreases the odds.







TipClinical Examples




Fasting Glucose (\(x_1\) in \(\text{mg/dL}\)):
From our fitted model: \(\theta_1 \approx 0.201 \longrightarrow \text{OR} = e^{0.201} \approx 1.223\).
Every \(+1\,\text{mg/dL}\) increase in glucose multiplies the odds of diabetes by \(1.223\) (a \(+22.3\%\) increase in odds).
Body Mass Index (\(x_2\) in \(\text{kg/m}^2\)):
\(\theta_{\text{bmi}} = 0.16 \longrightarrow \text{OR} = e^{0.16} \approx 1.174\).
Every \(+1\,\text{kg/m}^2\) increase in BMI multiplies the odds of diabetes by \(1.174\) (a \(+17.4\%\) increase).

title: 06 Logistic Regression: Classification
text:
5. A New Loss Function

5.1 MSE Problem for Classification
Plugging in the sigmoid \(\hat{y}_i = \sigma(x_i^T \theta)\) directly into mean squared error yields:
\[S(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left( y_i - \hat{y}_i \right)^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left( y_i - \sigma(x_i^T \theta) \right)^2\]
For a model with two features (\(x_{i1}, x_{i2}\)) and parameters \(\theta = (\theta_1, \theta_2)^T\), the linear predictor is \(x_i^T \theta = \theta_1 x_{i1} + \theta_2 x_{i2}\), giving the concrete loss:
\[S(\theta_1, \theta_2) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left( y_i - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta_1 x_{i1} + \theta_2 x_{i2})}} \right)^2\]

Non-Convexity: The composition of the quadratic loss with the non-linear sigmoid generates an irregular landscape with local minima and saddle points.
Gradient Saturation: When the model makes a confident wrong prediction (e.g. \(y=1\) but \(z \ll 0\)), the derivative \(\sigma'(z) \to 0\), causing updates to vanish and learning to stall.



Plot Contour Map of Loss Function (MSE)
# Concrete observations: 6 patients with two standardized clinical features (x_i1, x_i2)
X_sample = np.array([
    [ 0.5, -0.2],
    [-2.6, -2.7],
    [-1.1,  2.4],
    [-2.7,  2.4],
    [-2.3, -2.6],
    [-1.3,  0.7]
])
y_sample = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0])


t1 = np.linspace(-3, 3, 2000)
t2 = np.linspace(-3, 3, 2000)
T1, T2 = np.meshgrid(t1, t2)

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# S(theta) = 1/n sum (y_i - sigma(x_i^T theta))^2 where x_i^T theta = theta1 * x_i1 + theta2 * x_i2
Z = np.zeros_like(T1)
for (x1, x2), yi in zip(X_sample, y_sample):
    z = T1 * x1 + T2 * x2
    p = sigmoid(z)
    Z += (yi - p)**2
Z /= len(y_sample)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.2))
contour = ax.contourf(T1, T2, Z, levels=25, cmap='viridis')
ax.contour(T1, T2, Z, levels=20, colors='white', linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.4)
cbar = plt.colorbar(contour, ax=ax, pad=0.03)
cbar.set_label(r"Loss $S(\theta)$", fontsize=11)

ax.set_title("Contour map of loss function (MSE)", fontsize=12, pad=10)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_1$", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\theta_2$", fontsize=11)
ax.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5: Contour map of the Mean Squared Error loss \(S(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left( y_i - \sigma(\theta_1 x_{i1} + \theta_2 x_{i2}) \right)^2\), showing multiple local minima, saddle regions, and plateaus.








5.2 Deriving Binary Cross-Entropy
Because \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\), each observation follows an independent Bernoulli trial with success parameter \(\hat{y}_i = \sigma(x_i^T \theta)\):
\[P(y_i \mid x_i) = \hat{y}_i^{y_i} (1 - \hat{y}_i)^{1 - y_i}\]
For \(n\) independent observations, the joint Likelihood is:
\[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \hat{y}_i^{y_i} (1 - \hat{y}_i)^{1 - y_i}\]
Taking the negative logarithm (and normalizing by \(n\)) produces the loss function \(\ell(\theta)\):
\[\ell(\theta) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \ln \hat{y}_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \hat{y}_i) \right]\]


Plot Binary Cross-Entropy Loss Curves
p_vals = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 300)
loss_y1 = -np.log(p_vals)
loss_y0 = -np.log(1 - p_vals)

Plot Contour Map of Loss Function (BCE)
Z_bce = np.zeros_like(T1)
eps = 1e-12
for (x1, x2), yi in zip(X_sample, y_sample):
    z = T1 * x1 + T2 * x2
    p = np.clip(sigmoid(z), eps, 1 - eps)

Z_bce /= len(y_sample)

contour_bce = ax.contourf(T1, T2, Z_bce, levels=25, cmap='viridis')

ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_1$", fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\theta_2$", fontsize=11)
ax.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.5)

plt.show()

Convexity Guarantee: \(\ell(\theta)\) is strictly convex in \(\theta\) \(\to\) easier optimization

title: 13 Generating Randomness
text:
Before coming to this lecture, please complete the following:

Watch Video: Ben Lambert - The Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm
Pre-Reading: Marc Peter Deisenroth et al. (2020), Mathematics for Machine Learning, Section 6.5 (Sampling).
Probability Review: Concept of probability density functions (PDF) and cumulative distribution functions (CDF).






The Core Question: How can a completely deterministic machine generate a “random” number?
Algorithmic State: Every computer action is a predictable sequence of state changes.
The Solution: We simulate randomness using mathematical functions that “shuffle” states.

4. Theory: Summary
Recap: [Uniform distributions, CDFs, change of variables]

Linear Congruential Generator (LCG): \[X_{n+1} = (a X_n + c) \bmod m\]

title: 13 Generating Randomness
text:
5. Implementations and Illustrations
Metropolis-Hastings MCMC implementation:
import numpy as np

# Metropolis-Hastings for target p(x) ~ exp(-0.5 * x^2)
def metropolis_hastings(n_samples=5000, width=0.5):
    samples = np.zeros(n_samples)
    curr = 0.0
    for i in range(1, n_samples):
        prop = curr + np.random.normal(0, width)
        ratio = np.exp(-0.5 * prop**2) / np.exp(-0.5 * curr**2)
        if np.random.rand() < min(1.0, ratio):
            curr = prop
        samples[i] = curr
    return samples

title: Correlations
text:
Variable Relationships
To quantify associations between paired continuous variables, we evaluate two complementary correlation measures:

Pearson Correlation Coefficient (\(r_{xy} \in [-1, 1]\)): Measures strictly linear association: \[r_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(x, y)}{s_x s_y}\] In vector form with mean-centered vectors \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} - \bar{x}\mathbf{1}\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}\): \[r_{xy} = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^T \tilde{\mathbf{y}}}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\|_2 \|\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\|_2} = \cos(\phi)\]
Spearman Rank Correlation (\(r_s \in [-1, 1]\)): Evaluates monotonic association by computing Pearson’s formula on the ranks \(R(x)\) and \(R(y)\): \[r_s = 1 - \frac{6 \sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2}{n(n^2 - 1)}, \qquad d_i = R(x_i) - R(y_i)\] Spearman’s \(r_s\) assesses whether variables increase together regardless of whether the trend is linear, and is substantially more robust to extreme outliers.



Code
x = df_clean['insulin']
y = df_clean['glucose']
r_pearson = x.corr(y, method='pearson')
r_spearman = x.corr(y, method='spearman')

# Panel 1: Raw Observation Space (Pearson)
axes[0].scatter(x, y, alpha=0.45, color='#1f77b4', edgecolors='none', s=35)
axes[0].set_title(f'Raw Clinical Space: Pearson $r = {r_pearson:.3f}$', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Insulin [µU/ml]')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Glucose [mg/dL]')
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Panel 2: Rank Space (Spearman)

ry = y.rank()
axes[1].scatter(rx, ry, alpha=0.45, color='#2ca02c', edgecolors='none', s=35)
axes[1].set_title(f'Rank Space: Spearman $r_s = {r_spearman:.3f}$', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Rank(Insulin)')

Figure 2: Insulin vs. Glucose: Comparing linear Pearson correlation in raw clinical space (left) with monotonic Spearman rank correlation in rank space (right).











NotePearson versus Spearman




Sensitivity to High-Leverage Outliers: Pearson correlation operates on squared Euclidean distances. Extreme insulin observations (reaching up to \(846\ \mu\text{U/ml}\)) pull on the linear fit and attenuate sample covariance.
Biological Saturation: Cellular glucose response naturally exhibits saturation (diminishing return at high insulin concentrations). Rank transformation straightens monotonic curvature, bounding extreme outliers and capturing the true strength of biological co-regulation.
Attention — Single Summary Metrics: Both numbers are just single scalar values attempting to summarize potentially complex bivariate data structures. Neither number should be considered “true”, and both have distinct limitations:

Ties and excessive zeros: When datasets contain many identical zero values (e.g., missing records, detection limits, or single-cell dropouts), rank assignment can heavily skew Spearman’s rank correlation.
Isolated extreme outliers: A single extreme bivariate outlier can heavily inflate or deflate sample covariance, creating the illusion of a very strong or falsely absent Pearson correlation. Always inspect the bivariate scatter plot rather than relying blindly on a single correlation coefficient.

Dimension
